subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
subtype: Approach: setting a specific measurable target [Thinking]
passage: Monday night. “Get fitter” has never worked for me. It's too soft; I can always say I'm fitter than yesterday without doing anything. So I wrote real numbers on the inside of my diary cover. Goal: run 5 km without stopping at the school race on 14 December. Now: I can run 1 km before I have to walk. Plan: lengthen each week's run by roughly a quarter of a kilometre. Parveen ma'am checked it after PE and said it was the first time a student had written a date and a starting distance. It felt a little silly, then a little exciting, because for the first time I could tell exactly how far away 5 km was. — Sarika

qa.q: What is Sarika's starting distance?
qa.a: One kilometre, before having to walk.

qa.q: How does Sarika feel about the written plan?
qa.a: A little silly at first, then excited and hopeful, because the numbers show exactly how far the goal is.

qa.q: What else could Sarika do to keep going, and why?
qa.a: Write down each run's distance in the diary, since seeing the small gains builds confidence on tired days.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Parveen ma'am?
qa.a: Parveen ma'am sees a student who set a date and a starting point, which makes the goal specific and easier to coach.

grounding: A teen writes a date, a starting distance and a weekly increase for a 5 km run.

subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
subtype: Approach: progressive plan with rest days [Action]
passage: PE teacher's note, Friday. Gopika brought her running diary to show me. She does a run-and-walk session on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, with rest days between, and writes each one down: how far, how it felt, how her legs were the next day. In week four she told me she wanted to add two extra kilometres in one go, because she felt strong. I asked what her legs had said in the diary. She looked again and said, “A bit tight after Wednesday.” She kept to the plan and added only a little more distance. I told her that if a pain keeps going or worries her, she should tell me and see a doctor. I'll read the diary again next Friday. — Suraj

qa.q: How many days a week does Gopika run and walk?
qa.a: Three days a week, with rest days between.

qa.q: How might Gopika have felt when she wanted to add two extra kilometres?
qa.a: Eager and impatient because she felt strong, but she still held to the plan after reading her diary.

qa.q: What should Gopika do if a pain keeps going, and why?
qa.a: Tell the PE teacher and see a doctor, since pain that keeps going or worries her should be checked rather than pushed through.

qa.q: How does the diary look to Suraj?
qa.a: Suraj sees a written record, which makes it easier to notice early if the distance rises too fast.

grounding: A student follows a run-and-walk schedule with rest days, records each session and increases distance slowly.

subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
subtype: Approach: getting coaching from a qualified person [Action]
passage: Jayant had four videos open, each showing a different bowling drill from a different stranger. The trials were nine days away, and his shoulder had felt tight since he copied the fastest drill. Instead of watching a fifth video, he stayed after practice and asked Sabina ma'am, the school coach, to watch his action. She filmed it and showed him two small changes. Then she gave him a warm-up for his age and body: arm circles, light throws, easy jogging. “The drills you found are for fully grown bowlers,” she said. “Do these two things, come back on Thursday, and tell me how the shoulder feels.” Jayant nodded, oddly relieved. Someone had looked at him, not at a stranger's video.

qa.q: What did Sabina ma'am give Jayant?
qa.a: A warm-up for his age and body and two small changes to his action.

qa.q: How might Jayant have felt on hearing the online drills were for fully grown bowlers?
qa.a: Surprised and relieved: it explained the tight shoulder, and someone had finally looked at him and not at a video.

qa.q: What should Jayant do if the shoulder still hurts, and why?
qa.a: Rest, tell the coach and check with a doctor if it keeps going or worries him, since a tight shoulder should not be ignored before trials.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Sabina ma'am?
qa.a: Sabina ma'am sees an eager young bowler at risk of copying drills unsuited to his body, and is glad that he asked before something got worse.

grounding: A young cricketer asks the school coach to check his action and warm-up instead of copying online drills.

subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
passage: Coach's note, Thursday. For three weeks two of my students, Sachin and Shreya, have been at the ground before six every morning. They made a deal: the one who skips pays for the other's chai. On Tuesday the cold was sharp, and Sachin's message read, “I'm not coming.” Shreya replied, “Then you're buying my chai and a very good story.” Twenty minutes later Sachin arrived at the gate, hands in sleeves, muttering. The pair jogged, then sat with tea in the grass. I did nothing except unlock the gate. Neither of them would have come alone on Tuesday, and they know it. I've noticed their warm-ups are getting longer and more careful, and they laugh at the start. — Coach

qa.q: What does the one who skips pay for?
qa.a: The other's chai.

qa.q: What might Sachin have been feeling on the cold Tuesday?
qa.a: Reluctant to leave the warm bed, but also not wanting to let Shreya down.

qa.q: What else could the pair do to keep the habit going, and why?
qa.a: Agree on a backup plan for rain or very cold days, since weather is the easiest excuse to skip.

qa.q: How does the rule look to Shreya?
qa.a: Shreya finds that the deal makes skipping costly and turns the morning into something shared, which makes it easier to get up.

grounding: Two friends agree to meet at the ground at six, and the one who skips pays for the other's chai.

subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
subtype: Approach: doing too much too soon [Pitfall]
passage: “Disha, you asked how I ended up on the bench, so here it is. I'm Aman, and I wanted the school football team more than anything. I thought more was better. From day one I trained twice a day, once before school, once after. My legs felt sore by the third day. I told myself sore meant working. When my thigh started pulling, I taped it and carried on. In week two something gave way on the field, a proper strain. The coach said I needed rest and should see a doctor if it kept going. I missed the whole trial period. I wanted to speed everything up, and it cost me weeks instead of saving me any.”

qa.q: How many times a day did Aman train?
qa.a: Twice a day.

qa.q: How does Aman feel now about the choice?
qa.a: Frustrated and regretful: wanting to hurry things up cost weeks instead of saving them.

qa.q: What could Aman do differently next time, and why?
qa.a: Build up slowly with rest days and listen to soreness, since steady training keeps Aman on the field.

qa.q: How does the injury look to Aman's coach?
qa.a: Aman's coach sees an eager player who ignored warning signs, and probably wishes Aman had spoken up when the soreness began.

grounding: A teen aiming for the school team trains twice daily from day one, ignores soreness and picks up a strain.

subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
subtype: Approach: comparing with online influencers and extreme diets [Pitfall]
passage: Damini had watched the fitness influencer's videos for a week: a crash routine, three workouts a day, and a list of foods to cut. Damini copied all of it. By Thursday, everything felt slower. The stairs were hard. In the morning assembly the floor seemed to tilt. During maths, Damini's hands went cold and the board blurred. “Are you all right?” Vishal Sir asked, and helped Damini to a chair, then walked with Damini to the school nurse and rang home. The nurse said that growing bodies need enough food and proper advice from a doctor or qualified dietitian, not from videos. Damini listened, embarrassed, holding a glass of water, and thought about how quickly a promise of results had become a whole week of feeling awful.

qa.q: What did Damini feel in maths class?
qa.a: Damini's hands went cold and the board blurred.

qa.q: What did Damini want from copying the influencer's routine?
qa.a: To feel strong and look fit quickly, and to match the polished picture the videos promised.

qa.q: What could Damini do instead, and why?
qa.a: Ask a doctor, a coach or a qualified dietitian for advice suited to a growing body, since a video cannot know what one person needs.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Vishal Sir?
qa.a: Vishal Sir sees a student unwell after copying extreme advice, so he is concerned and wants the nurse and family involved straight away.

grounding: A student copies a fitness influencer's crash routine and food restrictions, feels weak and dizzy, and learns that growing bodies need adequate food and expert guidance.

subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
subtype: Approach: listening to the body and adapting [Revision]
passage: Day 21. My knee twinged after Sunday's road run, and it did again today, even before I started. The plan says ten kilometres this week, but my knee says otherwise. I know this isn't how you win. So I decided to listen. I cut Wednesday's run to half, took it to the soft school field, and stayed off the road. After practice I showed Tenzin Sir, our coach, my shoes. He turned them over and said the soles were worn flat. He also said, “If it keeps going or worries you, check with a doctor.” New plan: short runs on grass, then slowly longer again. It's a bit frustrating to go backwards, but I'd rather do that than stop completely. — Keerthana

qa.q: Where did Keerthana move the runs to?
qa.a: The soft school field, away from the road.

qa.q: How does Keerthana feel about changing the plan?
qa.a: A bit frustrated at going backwards but sensible: listening to the knee feels better than stopping completely.

qa.q: What should Keerthana do if the knee keeps hurting, and why?
qa.a: Check with a doctor, as Tenzin Sir said, since pain that keeps going or worries you needs a professional opinion.

qa.q: How does the change look to Tenzin Sir?
qa.a: Tenzin Sir is probably glad the pain was reported early and that the runner is adjusting instead of hiding it.

grounding: A teen notices knee pain on hard roads, cuts distance, moves to a softer field, asks the coach about shoes and returns gradually.

subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
subtype: Approach: planning around exams and study load [Thinking]
passage: Six weeks to boards. Old me: an hour of running, then guilt about not studying, then studying badly because of the guilt. New thinking, written down so I'll remember it: movement isn't a rival of marks; it's part of how I stay sharp. I've noticed I remember chapters better after a walk. So the plan is twenty minutes at 5:30 every evening, fixed, not longer. After two hours of study, five minutes of stretching. That's it. No hour-long runs until boards are done. My sister Hafsa said she would join for the skipping. I don't feel I'm giving up sport. I feel like I've found the size of it that fits this season. — Seema

qa.q: How long are Seema's exercise sessions now?
qa.a: Twenty minutes, fixed at 5:30 every evening.

qa.q: How does Seema now feel about exercise during exams?
qa.a: Relieved and less guilty: the shorter fixed slots feel like the right size for this season.

qa.q: What else could Seema do on the heaviest study days, and why?
qa.a: Keep just a short walk instead of skipping movement completely, since even a little keeps the habit and clears the head.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Hafsa?
qa.a: Hafsa sees Seema still moving instead of giving up sport, and joining for the skipping lets Hafsa help without adding pressure.

grounding: A teen with board exams shortens exercise to twenty minutes in fixed slots, treating movement as a study aid.

subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
subtype: Approach: process goals when results stall [Revision]
passage: At the athletics club, Shreya checked the stopwatch again: 14.2 seconds for the hundred metres, the same as the last five weeks. She kicked the starting block and sat on the track. Coach Sarika ma'am crouched beside her. “What is the clock telling you?” “That I'm stuck.” “What can you control?” Shreya thought. “Coming to every session. Doing the start drill properly. Keeping my arms low.” Sarika ma'am handed her a card. “Track those, not the time. Tick each one.” For a month Shreya ticked boxes for attendance, the start drill and arm position, and stopped staring at the clock. In the fifth week she ran 14.0, and hardly noticed she'd stopped worrying.

qa.q: What did Shreya start tracking instead of her time?
qa.a: Attendance, the start drill and arm position.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel about her stalled sprint time?
qa.a: Stuck and frustrated: she kicked the starting block and sat down on the track.

qa.q: What else could Shreya do to check her technique, and why?
qa.a: Have a friend film her start each week, since seeing the drill helps her correct what the clock cannot show.

qa.q: How does the change look to Sarika ma'am?
qa.a: Sarika ma'am sees a runner fixed on the stopwatch and steers her toward things she can control, so she can stay motivated between improvements.

grounding: After a plateau in her sprint time, a student tracks attendance and technique drills, and progress returns.

subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
subtype: Approach: visualising the race and rehearsing [Thinking]
passage: The night before the district meet, Preeti lay on her bed with her eyes closed. She walked herself through the day. Arrive early. Warm-up: light jog, drills, two short strides. At the line, feet in the blocks, wait for the gun. Then the first ten steps, low and quick, and the long push to the final stretch. Then the part she'd rarely rehearsed: what if she stumbled? She'd shorten the next stride, keep her eyes on the finish line, and not look at the others. Last, the breathing Bhupen Sir had taught her: in for four, out for six, three times. Her hands unclenched. She opened her eyes. It was only practice in her head, but her chest felt quieter.

qa.q: What would Preeti do if she stumbled?
qa.a: Shorten the next stride, keep her eyes on the finish line and not look at the others.

qa.q: How was Preeti feeling before the race, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Nervous but steadying: her hands unclenched and her chest felt quieter after the mental walk-through.

qa.q: What else could Preeti do to make the rehearsal stronger, and why?
qa.a: Walk the real track before the meet, since seeing the actual surface and lines makes the mental picture more accurate.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Bhupen Sir?
qa.a: Bhupen Sir sees his athlete using the breathing he taught, so he may feel proud and reassured that she is calm before the meet.

grounding: An athlete mentally walks through the warm-up, start and final stretch, plans for a stumble and steadies herself with a set breathing pattern.
